slides.title: Straight lines: _y_ = _m__x_ + _c_
slides.lede: A straight line is a constant rate of change. Its rule tells you how steep it is and where it starts, and its picture shows you both at once.

groups.title: Gradient
groups.lede: Gradient is a rate: how far up for how far across. Any two points on the line give the same answer.

examples.label: A line that rises
examples.prompt: Find the gradient of the line through (1, 2) and (5, 5).

steps.text: Write the gradient as rise over run.
Subtract in the same order top and bottom. Second point minus first, both times.
Work out each subtraction, then simplify.

examples.answer: _m_ = 3/4 — the line rises 3 for every 4 across.

examples.label: A line that falls
examples.prompt: Find the gradient of the line through (−2, 4) and (4, 0).

steps.text: Substitute, keeping the brackets around the negative coordinate.
Subtracting a negative adds. The run is 6, not 2.
Simplify. A negative gradient means the line falls as _x_ increases.

examples.answer: _m_ = −2/3 — the line falls 2 for every 3 across.

relations.body: Both examples used the same subtraction in the same order. Reversing one of them, but not the other, is the mistake to watch for: it turns a rise into a fall.

groups.title: Where the line crosses

steps.text: Put _x_ = 0 to find where it crosses the _y_-axis.
Put _y_ = 0 to find where it crosses the _x_-axis.
Solve for _x_. The answer is a fraction, and that is normal.

groups.lede: Put one variable to zero and the other one falls out. Two substitutions give both intercepts.

relations.body: Reading the rule for the _y_-intercept is quicker than the working: in _y_ = _m__x_ + _c_ the number on its own IS where the line crosses. The working is here because the _x_-intercept has no such shortcut.

groups.title: From a rule to a picture

examples.label: Plotting _y_ = 2_x_ − 1

steps.text: Choose whole values of _x_ across the range you were given, and work out each _y_.
Plot the pairs and join them. If one point is off the line, it is that point’s arithmetic that is wrong, not the rule.

examples.answer: A straight line through (0, −1), going up 2 for every 1 across.

groups.lede: Two points fix a straight line. The third one is the check that you have not made an arithmetic slip.

relations.label: Reading the line against the table
items: Every pair in the table is a point on the line, and every point on the line is a pair that would fit the table.
Going one step right along the table adds 2 to _y_ every time. That constant step IS the gradient.
The column for _x_ = 0 holds −1, and that is where the line crosses the _y_-axis.

groups.title: Comparing steepness
groups.lede: Three lines through the same point on the _y_-axis, so the only thing that differs is the gradient.

relations.label: What the three show
items: All three meet at (0, 1), because all three rules end in + 1. The intercept is the constant.
The steepest climb is _m_ = 2: one across, two up. Half the gradient is half the climb for the same step.
The third gradient is negative, so the line falls. Its steepness is still 1 — the sign says direction, the size says steepness.
A gradient of 0 would be flat, and a vertical line has no gradient at all: the run would be zero, and you cannot divide by it.
